analysis.one_liner: Taxes at 100 percent the money banks recover from tax-shelter lease deals with public agencies and ends their litigation cost write-offs.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Finance Committee in 2009 without a vote, leaving the tax-shelter dispute untouched.
analysis.plain_summary: Sale-in/lease-out (SILO) and lease-in/lease-out (LILO) deals were tax shelters in which big banks claimed large tax benefits by paying public transit agencies to buy rail assets and lease them back. The IRS disallowed these benefits, so banks pursued lawsuits and settlements against the public agencies to claw the money back. This bill would have imposed a 100 percent excise tax on those clawback proceeds and denied banks a tax deduction for the attorney fees they spent enforcing the shelters, effectively ending the litigation strategy while leaving the public lessees out of the tax.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal taxpayers, because the bill would keep tax-shelter proceeds from flowing back to the banks that used them. It also protects tax-exempt public entities like transit agencies that were the nominal lessees in these deals, since the bill's excise tax explicitly excludes them.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a 100 percent excise tax equal to the full amount of any proceeds a bank receives from litigation or settlement over a SILO or LILO transaction, so clawing back shelter proceeds would yield nothing.
Explicitly excludes the tax-exempt or nonprofit lessee — typically the public transit agency — from the excise tax, so the tax falls on the shelter users, not the public entities.
Denies any tax deduction for attorney fees and other costs of litigation brought to recover proceeds from these transactions, raising the cost of enforcing the shelters.

Contains anti-avoidance rules — it disregards transfers of rights that would shift the tax to someone else, lets Treasury write regulations to prevent evasion, and stacks the excise tax on top of any other tax or penalty.

analysis.who_pays: The financial institutions that used SILO and LILO shelters and were seeking to recover their proceeds through litigation and settlements would lose those recoveries and could no longer deduct the legal costs of pursuing them.

drawbacks.text: The excise tax reaches amounts received after introduction, including proceeds from consensual terminations and rescissions of deals that the parties had already negotiated, which could disrupt settled arrangements between banks and public agencies.

Denying a deduction for attorney fees means the government taxes the gross recovery of amounts a bank was contesting, a blunt instrument that applies even when a bank believed its position had legal merit — opponents could fairly call it a penalty that predetermines the dispute.
Because the tax applies only to these two named shelter types identified in specific IRS notices, it does nothing about the broader class of similar lease-based tax shelters.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was aimed at a well-documented tax shelter whose losers were the federal Treasury and, through clawback litigation, the public agencies that had entered the deals. The trade-offs were narrow: it could upend settlements already negotiated and its full tax on litigation recoveries is punitive by design, but the main benefit — closing out roughly a billion-dollar shelter category — clearly outweighed those costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in June 2009, referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and never reported out or brought to the floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill defines SILO transactions as the sale-leaseback arrangements identified as listed transactions in IRS Notice 2005-13, and LILO transactions as lease-in/lease-out deals identified in IRS Notice 2000-15, closing in on specific shelter types the IRS had already flagged.

The excise tax applies to any party that receives an 'ineligible amount' — the excess of proceeds recovered through remedial litigation, consensual termination, or rescission over amounts recovered from third-party defeasance arrangements — at a rate of 100 percent, meaning the entire recovery is taken by the government.
Separately, the bill adds a section to the tax code denying any deduction for attorney fees or other costs of litigation to recover these proceeds, on top of the excise tax.

It was introduced by Senator Menendez on June 24, 2009 and referred the same day to the Senate Finance Committee; the action history shows no markup, no committee vote, no floor action, and no roll call before the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.
Four Democratic senators cosponsored the bill, all in the first days after introduction, and no Republican cosponsored.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The financial institutions that had used SILO and LILO shelters — they kept their litigation and settlement recoveries free of any new tax, and the costs of enforcing the shelters remained deductible.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The banks that used the shelters

for.name: Robert Menendez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and made introductory remarks on June 24, 2009.

for.name: 4 of 58 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill shortly after introduction.

against.name: Max Baucus
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration; the action history shows nothing after the June 2009 referral.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so there is no roll call; all five sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on, but whether the committee inaction reflected party opposition or simply low priority cannot be determined from the record.

industries.industry: Large financial institutions and banks that used SILO/LILO shelters
industries.note: These institutions had claimed large tax benefits under the deals; after the IRS disallowed them, they pursued litigation and settlements to recover the proceeds, including from the public transit agencies that were the nominal lessees. The bill would have taxed those recoveries at 100 percent and denied deductions for the legal costs of pursuing them, ending the recovery strategy.

industries.industry: Public transit agencies and other tax-exempt lessees
industries.note: They had received large upfront payments from banks in the original deals and became the target of clawback litigation when the IRS disallowed the shelters. The bill would have shielded them by taxing the banks' recoveries at 100 percent and explicitly exempting the tax-exempt lessee from the tax.

industries.industry: The federal Treasury and general taxpayers
industries.note: The bill would have prevented shelter proceeds from flowing back to the banks, preserving federal tax revenue. It contains no other spending mechanism.
